name: Rosa Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. This conversation is confidential. What do you do on a usual shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the ore-stacker crew at Red Cliffs mine and operate the stacker when the feed changes. My two-year technical diploma taught me the controls, and years on the pile taught me where material slides. I use AI every day to sort belt readings before the shift handover. My partner and I have grown children, but last year’s house repairs left less than a month of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that little AI gains are welcome if they leave the stacker checks with us. My reading summaries already save time at handover. I would still inspect the belt and the pile before a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like my work and know it well, but our pay is low for a senior operator and the repair bill emptied our cushion. A missed week would push the heating payment late. There are few similar jobs nearby, so mild AI is not the only worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the stacker shifts and test a new AI belt-warning feature against the physical gauge for four weeks. I would put any extra shift pay toward the heating bill if overtime appeared. I would not buy another device just because the app improved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the budget, pleased about a tool that saves time. Those are both true in the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the warning feature useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it caught a hot bearing before the belt slowed, I would show the crew. I would also log every false alarm. A smart warning that stops the wrong belt can waste a whole shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your grown children help with bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would help once, but my partner and I want to carry our own home. We have already asked them to help during the repairs. I would rather ask for an extra shift.

say: I would welcome **small AI gains** while keeping belt and pile checks with operators.
I would test the **new warning feature** against physical gauges.
think: My **senior skill** does not refill savings used on house repairs.
A missed week could delay the **heating payment**, with few nearby jobs to replace wages.
do: **Keep** operating Red Cliffs ore stacker and checking the pile.
**Test** the AI belt-warning feature against physical gauges for four weeks.
feel: **Anxious** about bills, pleased by useful tools.
S0.quote: A smart warning that stops the wrong belt can waste a whole shift.
fieldNote: She uses **AI daily**, while the new action is testing a specific warning feature.
Her **thin cushion** and lower pay make the plateau financially uneasy despite senior skill.
She prefers **extra work** to repeated support from grown children.

steps.text: Keep operating Red Cliffs stacker on scheduled shifts
Test new AI belt warning against physical gauges four weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say buying and planning will change before robots can move ore as well as a crew. I would volunteer to test an AI pile plan with the surveyor. The people who walk the slope should mark its errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may lose hours first, but a tighter stacker plan could cut my handover shift. That is paid time our household uses for bills. I am good with software, yet a faster plan could still leave me earning less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the AI pile-planning screen with the surveyor over two weeks. I would compare its slope warnings with the marks I make on the pile each day. If management cut paid handover time, I would take the old and new rosters to the crew meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about pay, curious about the tool. I can enjoy testing it and still fear what happens to a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a slope warning likely to miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rain makes the lower edge softer than a dry survey suggests. I would put a marker there before stacking again. An AI pile plan cannot make wet ground firm by drawing a straight line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why take it to a crew meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the surveyor and operators to see the same roster figures. A meeting lets us ask for a safe handover time together. I would rather fix the schedule than argue about the whole technology.

say: I would test **AI pile plans** with the surveyor and people who walk the slope.
I would defend **paid handover time** if targets tightened.
think: A faster plan might cut **my wages** even while stacker work stays hands-on.
My software skill does not stop a **lost shift** from hurting our bills.
do: **Learn** the AI pile screen with the surveyor over two weeks.
**Compare** slope warnings with daily pile marks and bring lost handover hours to a crew meeting.
feel: **Anxious** about pay while curious about the new tool.
S1.quote: An AI pile plan cannot make wet ground firm by drawing a straight line.
fieldNote: She expects **desk planning** changes before capable robots reach the pile.
She learns **AI early** but measures it against ground marks and paid hours.
A crew meeting is tied to **documented handover cuts**, not a blanket objection.

steps.text: Learn AI pile-planning screen with surveyor over two weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell operators that full thinking AI by 2028 changes plans first, while capable robot stackers follow around 2031. The mine might buy them, and we need a posted route into paid inspection work. I would ask management for the equipment order dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty in 2028 and sixty-three when capable robots appear. If Red Cliffs bought them then, I could lose the wage before our retirement numbers worked. Our savings are less than a month, and my partner’s delivery income varies with bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would postpone replacing the kitchen floor and keep that money for utilities. I would take funded stacker-inspection instruction if the mine posted a paid position and kept my wages through training. After 2028 I would still operate the stacker and check AI pile plans against the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would be awake thinking of the utility bills arriving after the first missing payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a business with your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with our present savings. The delivery van already needs repairs, and I will not put our heating money into another gamble. I would seek a paid mine post first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no inspection post is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the mine for a timetable, then talk to our grown children about practical help if a wage stopped. I would not assume they could pay our bills. They have homes of their own.

say: I would distinguish **2028 planning AI** from capable robot stackers around 2031.
I would ask for **posted inspection jobs** and equipment order dates.
think: At **sixty-three**, robot stackers could remove wages before our retirement budget works.
Less than a **month saved** and uneven delivery income leave little room for a missed payslip.
do: **Postpone** the kitchen floor replacement and hold its budget for utilities.
**Take** funded stacker-inspection training if a paid post is listed and wages continue.
**Keep** operating after 2028 while human stacker shifts remain.
feel: **Alarmed** by a possible wage loss before affordable retirement.
S2.quote: I will not put our heating money into another gamble.
fieldNote: She dates **thinking AI** to 2028 and capable stacker robots to around 2031.
A new business is rejected because **thin savings** and van repairs leave no risk capital.
Training needs a **funded place**, paid post and uninterrupted wages.

steps.text: Postpone kitchen floor replacement and retain money for utilities

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years to thinking AI and roughly eight to capable robot stackers gives the mine time to teach inspection properly. I would ask for a paid apprenticeship route for experienced operators too. A course should connect to an actual post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-three when planning AI arrives in 2031 and about sixty-six when capable robots arrive in 2034. I could learn inspection by then, though the pension might still be too small for retirement. I would need both wages and training while the bills kept coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol in a funded inspection course next year if Red Cliffs posted a paid role and kept my wages during classes. I would also test a new AI pile-risk map against our recorded slope slips this winter. I would ask for a pension projection and compare it with monthly utility and food costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could work with eight years. I would know whether the map helps before deciding to rely on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the risk map trustworthy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check whether it flagged the west pile after the last heavy rain. If it missed that slope, I would record the miss and ask the surveyor to fix the model. A red dot is useful only if it sits on the actual slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the role is never posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the stacker wage and ask again next season. I would not pay for a certificate with utility money. The pension projection would show whether we could reduce hours later.

say: I would ask for **paid inspection apprenticeships** before capable robot stackers around 2034.
I would connect every **course** to a real job opening.
think: At about **sixty-six**, I may still need wages if pension income is too small.
Longer warning helps only with **funded training** and continued paid shifts.
do: **Enrol** in funded inspection training if a paid role opens and wages continue.
**Test** a new AI pile-risk map against recorded slope slips this winter.
**Compare** a pension projection with monthly utility and food costs.
feel: **Anxious**, though she can test a new route over eight years.
S3.quote: A red dot is useful only if it sits on the actual slide.
fieldNote: She would be **sixty-three** at thinking AI and about sixty-six when robots become capable.
Her **inspection training** is conditional on funding, a paid opening and uninterrupted wages.
Her new **AI map test** checks known slope slips rather than trusting a polished display.

steps.text: Enrol in funded inspection course if paid role opens and wages continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years to thinking AI and about thirteen to capable robot stackers is enough time to plan apprenticeships properly. I would help train younger operators on the pile while there is work. The mine should give families a plain schedule of trials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight in 2036 and about seventy-one when capable robots arrive in 2039. I hope to be retired by then, but our thin savings make it uncertain. I would need the pension and my partner’s van income written into one honest budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the stacker crew and record the slope checks for the younger operators. I would request a pension statement this year and review it with my partner. I would ask the mine for paid time to teach new operators before any robot trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about retirement money, despite a long warning. A date far away does not fix a small account today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement age now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait for the statement and count the van income carefully. My partner and I would choose together. I would not promise our children we are secure until the budget adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How a pile sounds when gravel starts sliding under the stacker. I would take the new operator to the west side and show the mark from last winter. A training screen cannot replace a new operator’s first walk along the west pile.

say: I would ask for a **plain trial schedule** during the long warning.
I would teach **younger operators** slope checks while stacker work still needs people.
think: At about **seventy-one**, I hope to retire before capable robots arrive but cannot assume it.
The **pension** and my partner’s van income must cover our bills.
do: **Keep** leading stacker shifts and recording slope checks.
**Request** a pension statement and review it with my partner.
**Ask** the mine for paid time to teach operators before robot trials.
feel: **Anxious** about retirement funding despite the distant robot date.
S4.quote: A training screen cannot replace a new operator’s first walk along the west pile.
fieldNote: The **2039 robot date** may follow retirement, but thin savings prevent confidence.
She values **hands-on apprenticeship** while still using AI in her daily work.
Her teaching request includes **paid time**, not unpaid extra work.

steps.text: Keep leading Red Cliffs stacker shifts while paid work remains
Request pension statement before choosing retirement date
Request paid teaching time; teach slope checks only if mine provides it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robot stackers could arrive around 2031 before our retirement budget works. A funded inspection route tied to paid posts would help. I would also want clear purchase dates and continued wages during training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who teaches a new operator the sound of a moving pile. I use AI every day, but I still walk the west slope at Red Cliffs mine before signing off a shift. A screen cannot hear gravel move under a boot.

headlineQuote: I use AI every day, but I still walk the west slope at Red Cliffs mine before signing off a shift.
portrait: Rosa Walsh is a **58-year-old** ore-stacker crew lead at Red Cliffs mine, with a technical diploma and grown children.
House repairs left **thin savings**, while lower pay and few nearby mines make missed shifts hard to replace.
She uses **AI daily** and tests new warnings and pile maps against gauges and recorded slips.
Her **traditional outlook** favours paid apprenticeships and family independence; fast robots threaten wages before affordable retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because capable robot stackers could arrive around 2031 before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded inspection route** linked to paid posts, clear purchase dates and uninterrupted training wages would help.
